name: Alcove-Rust
geological_features: Iron-oxide alcove formations in eroded cliff faces
description: Alcove-Rust is a desert world stained every shade of red and brown by pervasive iron oxide, its cliff faces eroded into deep alcoves that provide shelter from the scouring winds. The alcoves are carved from alternating layers of hard and soft sedimentary rock, the softer layers dissolving to create recesses while the harder layers form protective overhangs. The dune fields between cliff systems are rust-red, their iron-rich sand fine enough to infiltrate any unsealed joint or closure.

The thin atmosphere is dry and carries a perpetual haze of iron dust that tints the sky a pale salmon and sunsets a deep, bruised crimson. The alcoves are the only sheltered spaces on the surface, their interiors cooler and calmer than the wind-blasted terrain outside. Deep within the largest alcoves, hematite crystals grow in clusters from the walls, their metallic surfaces reflecting light in geometric patterns. The overall mood is one of ancient, rusted grandeur.

Microbial life on Alcove-Rust is iron-dependent, metabolizing the abundant iron oxides through a chemolithotrophic process that slowly converts hematite to magnetite. These organisms coat the alcove walls in thin biofilms that are invisible to the naked eye but detectable through spectral analysis. Their metabolic activity over geological time has contributed to the layering patterns in the cliff faces, making them participants in the planet's geology as well as its biology.

Alcove-Rust's iron deposits are essentially planet-wide, making selective extraction straightforward. The hematite crystals in the cave systems have commercial value as industrial abrasives and decorative materials. The microbial iron metabolism has attracted interest from bio-mining researchers, as the organisms demonstrate a process that could be adapted for mineral processing. A small research outpost operates from one of the larger alcove systems.
